extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics students, and general readers interested in the nature, aesthetics, and evaluation of mathematical work
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria for judging and producing mathematical work (theorems, proofs, teaching, and the mathematician's practice) based on Hardy's A Mathematician's Apology: e.g., beauty, seriousness, generality, depth, proof-elegance, pedagogical posture, and usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching duty: amplify importance of subject and self
rubrics_metrics.description: It is one of the first duties of a professor ... to exaggerate a little both the importance of his subject and his own importance in it. A man who is always asking ‘Is what I do worth while?’ and ‘Am I the right person to do it?’ will always be ineffective himself and a discouragement to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professors should adopt a modest degree of self-importance and speak of their subject confidently to avoid paralyzing doubt in themselves and discouraging students; shut your eyes a little and think a little more of your subject and yourself than they deserve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immortality/permanence of mathematical ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes will be remembered when Aeschylus is forgotten, because languages die and mathematical ideas do not. 'Immortality' may be a silly word, but probably a mathematician has the best chance of whatever it may mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical ideas can endure beyond languages and epochs because they are embodied in theorems; however, this 'immortality' is relative and tied to the persistence of writings and concepts (fossilization of ideas as theorems). Be cautious of tautological appeals to 'mathematical reality'—the permanence depends on transmission and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as the first test of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematician, like a painter or a poet, is a maker of patterns ... Beauty is the first test: there is no permanent place in the world for ugly mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical work should produce harmonious patterns of ideas where the parts fit together; aesthetic appreciation is widespread (example: chess problems recognized as mathematical beauty). If mathematics is 'ugly' it is unlikely to have lasting value. Therefore aesthetic judgment should play a primary role in valuing mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance/seriousness: connecting significant ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The best mathematics is serious as well as beautiful ... The 'seriousness' of a mathematical theorem lies ... in the significance of the mathematical ideas which it connects. We may say ... that a mathematical idea is 'significant' if it can be connected, in a natural and illuminating way, with a large complex of other mathematical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theorems by how naturally and illuminatingly they link to a broad network of ideas. Serious theorems tend to lead to important advances in mathematics (and sometimes other sciences). Practical consequences are not the main measure; the pattern of connections is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality and depth (balance) for seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two things ... which seem essential [to significance], a certain generality and a certain depth; but neither quality is easy to define ... Some measure of generality must be present ... but too much tends inevitably to insipidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a 'large generalization, limited by a happy particularity'—sufficient generality to be fruitful but bounded by individuality that keeps the idea interesting. Depth is associated with lower/closer-to-foundation strata and more difficulty; both depth and well-calibrated generality make an idea significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty of proofs: unexpectedness, inevitability, economy, simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: In proofs ... there is a very high degree of unexpectedness, combined with inevitability and economy. The arguments take so odd and surprising a form; the weapons used seem so childishly simple ... There are no complications of detail—one line of attack is enough ... 'enumeration of cases' ... is one of the duller forms of mathematical arguments. A mathematical proof should resemble a simple and clear-cut constellation, not a scattered cluster in the Milky Way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs that are surprising yet inevitable, economical in means, and avoid needless complication or sprawling casework. Seek single clear lines of attack and structural clarity; while messy case analyses can be acceptable provisionally, elegance and conceptual unity are the ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on brute case enumeration (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Enumeration of cases' ... is one of the duller forms of mathematical arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat extensive case-splitting as a sign to look for a deeper, more unifying argument. Though such proofs are valid and can be useful, they lack the aesthetic qualities and explanatory power of more unified proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical objects are abstract; geometry is not pictorial physical reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The point important to us now is ... that pure geometries are not pictures, and that is the spatio-temporal reality of the physical world. Their function [figures] is merely to bring home meaning to hearers; they are pedagogical illustrations, not part of the real subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate geometric diagrams or physical intuitions with the subject-matter of pure geometry. Diagrams are aids for intuition and teaching; correctness of mathematical arguments does not depend on the fidelity of drawings to physical reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematician's subject-matter: internal mathematical reality distinct from physics
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematician, on the other hand, is working with his own mathematical reality. Physicists try to correlate facts with abstract schemes borrowed from mathematics, but mathematics constructs and works within its own abstract reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating mathematical work, recognize that its standards and objects are internally generated; success is judged by internal coherence, conceptual unity, and connection to other mathematical ideas rather than empirical correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a reserve of knowledge; value breadth ('useful' mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: We must ... remember that a reserve of knowledge is always an advantage, and that the most practical of mathematicians may be seriously handicapped if his knowledge is the minimum which is essential to him; and for that reason, we must add a little under every heading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage mathematicians (even those focused on applications) to cultivate more than the bare minimum relevant to their immediate needs. Broad background knowledge increases capability and avoids handicapping practical work.
